lesson.title: One Equation to Rule the Gases: PV = nRT
lesson.summary: The ideal gas law, PV = nRT, links pressure, volume, moles, and temperature into a single equation that describes how an idealized gas behaves under almost any condition.
lesson.body:
So far you have four separate ideas in hand: gases are particles in constant motion with negligible attraction between them, gas pressure comes from particle collisions, the mole concept lets you count particles by counting grams, and temperature scales let you track how much kinetic energy those particles have (always using Kelvin, never Celsius, for gas calculations, since Kelvin starts at absolute zero where particle motion theoretically stops). The ideal gas law combines all four of these into one relationship: PV = nRT, where P is pressure, V is volume, n is the number of moles, T is the absolute temperature in Kelvin, and R is a constant of proportionality called the ideal gas constant, covered in detail in the next chapter.

The reason this single equation works is that it is describing an idealized gas: one where the particles themselves take up no volume and exert no forces on each other except during a collision. Real gases behave very close to this ideal at ordinary temperatures and pressures, which is precisely because gas particles are so far apart, as you saw when comparing liquid water to steam. Under extreme conditions, very high pressure or very low temperature, real gases start to deviate from PV = nRT, because the particles get squeezed close enough for their actual size and their intermolecular attractions to matter. For the vast majority of chemistry problems, though, the ideal gas law is an excellent model.

The real power of PV = nRT is that if you know any three of the four variables, you can solve for the fourth. Suppose you have 2.00 mol of an ideal gas at a pressure of 1.50 atm and a temperature of 300 K, and you want to know what volume it occupies. Rearranging the equation to solve for V gives V = nRT / P. Using R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K), the calculation is: V = (2.00 mol)(0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K))(300 K) / (1.50 atm). Multiplying the numerator first: 0.0821 times 300 is 24.63, and 24.63 times 2.00 is 49.26. Dividing by the pressure: 49.26 / 1.50 = 32.8 L. So this sample of gas occupies about 32.8 liters.

Notice that the units all had to match the units built into R: pressure in atmospheres, volume in liters, amount in moles, temperature in Kelvin. Mismatched units are the single most common source of error in gas law problems, so it is worth developing the habit of writing every given value with its unit before you touch the equation. The next several chapters explore what happens to PV = nRT when you hold two of these four variables fixed and let the other two vary together; those relationships are Boyle's law, Charles's law, and Avogadro's law, and each one is really just a special case of the single equation you just learned.
